head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Ugly numbers are positive; 0 would loop forever (`0 % 2 == 0`) and negatives are excluded
Check a small fixed set of primes
Strip every factor of `p` (a loop, since p may divide many times)
If anything other than 2, 3, 5 divided n, a bigger factor remains
The leftover tells you whether another prime exists

p: `n = 30 = 2·3·5` strips down to 1 (ugly). `n = 14 = 2·7` leaves 7 (not ugly).
`8 = 2·2·2` needs three divisions by 2. With `if` you would divide once and be left with 4, wrongly rejecting it.

blocks.h: Why a leftover of 1 is the right test
p: After removing every 2, 3 and 5, the remaining value is a product of the other primes. It is 1 exactly when there were none, so equality with 1 decides it.

bullets: Time: O(log n), each division at least halves n.
Space: O(1).

263.takeaway: Strip out all factors of 2, 3 and 5 with while-loops; the number is ugly iff what remains is 1 (and n was positive).

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Map from character to its count
We don't care which character, only how many
1 for an odd count, 0 for even
How many characters have an odd count: at most one is allowed

p: `"carerac"`:

blocks.h: Why is 'at most one odd count' the right rule?
p: A palindrome pairs each character with its mirror. Characters with even counts pair up fully. A single character with an odd count can sit in the middle (odd length). Two odd counts would leave two unpaired characters; zero odd counts needs even length, which is automatically consistent.

blocks.h: Why no need to build the palindrome?
p: The question is only existence. Counting parity avoids generating permutations (factorial) entirely.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(k), k distinct characters (O(1) for a fixed alphabet).

266.takeaway: Palindrome permutation = at most one character with an odd frequency.

Order information only comes from neighbours in a sorted list
`for x, y in zip(a, b): if x != y: … break`
The first differing letter gives one rule `x < y`; later letters say nothing
The `else` runs only when the loop did NOT `break`, meaning one word is a prefix of the other
Detecting the prefix case without a flag
Characters with no remaining predecessors can come next
If some letters never reached in-degree 0 there is a cycle

p: Comparing neighbouring words gives these rules:
Start with letters that nothing must precede (`w`, `e` have in-degree 0 after edges `t→f`, `w→e`, `r→t`, `e→r`).. the queue evolves like this:

blocks.h: Why the `for … else` prefix check matters
blocks.p: Letters with no predecessor go first. Each time a letter is taken, its successors lose one unmet predecessor and join the queue when they reach zero.

bullets: Time: O(C), where C is the total number of characters in the words (building edges plus the sort).
Space: O(U + E) for the letters and edges.

269.takeaway: Alien dictionary = build a precedence graph from the first differing letters of adjacent words, then topologically sort it (Kahn); a cycle or prefix violation means no order.

A sliding window of the k consecutive in-order values closest to the target so far
Fixed-size window with O(1) removal from the front
Window not full yet: take the value
Is the new value closer than the oldest (smallest) one in the window? Then slide
The smallest value in the window is the furthest below the target
Not closer: every later value is larger and therefore even farther, so stop without visiting the right subtree

rows: not closer than oldest → stop (skip right subtree)

blocks.h: Why can we stop at the first value that is not closer?
p: The window holds consecutive in-order values, so `win[0]` is the smallest. Once a new value (larger than everything before) is not closer than `win[0]`, it must lie above the target and be farther from it than `win[0]`; all later values are larger still, so none can improve the window.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `citations[mid]` has `n - mid` papers with at least that many citations (itself and everything to its right)
Turn a sorted array into a counting statement
Predicate: this position already satisfies the h-index condition for h = `n - mid`
Find the first index where the predicate is true
Papers from `lo` onward qualify; if none qualify `lo = n` and the answer is 0
Converting the index back to a count

p: `citations = [0,1,3,5,6]`, `n = 5`. The predicate compares the value with the number of papers from that index to the end.
As `mid` increases, `citations[mid]` grows (sorted) and `n - mid` shrinks, so once `citations[mid] ≥ n - mid` is true it stays true. That is exactly what binary search requires.

blocks.h: Why it beats the unsorted version
p: Problem 274 sorts or counts in O(n). Here the input is already sorted, so O(log n) is possible; the answer `n - lo` is the largest h for which h papers have at least h citations.

bullets: Time: O(log n).
Space: O(1).

275.takeaway: H-index on a sorted array = binary search for the first index where `citations[i] >= n - i`; answer `n - index`.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Given API: costs one call; false for good versions, true for bad ones, and stays true afterwards
A monotone predicate: all False then all True
Search range of version numbers; the answer is guaranteed to be inside
`mid` could be the first bad one, so keep it
`mid` is good, so the answer is to the right

p: `n = 5`, first bad version is 4 (versions 4 and 5 are bad).

If `mid` is bad it might be the FIRST bad version; setting `hi = mid - 1` would throw it away. Keeping it in range and ending with `lo == hi` finds the boundary. Version `mid` being good is the only time we can exclude it.
In Python integers do not overflow. In Java/C++ write `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`, because `lo + hi` can exceed 2³¹ when `n` is near the limit; this is the classic follow-up.

bullets: Time: O(log n) calls to `isBadVersion` (minimising API calls is the point).
Space: O(1).

278.takeaway: Find the first True in a monotone False…True sequence: binary search with `hi = mid` on True and `lo = mid + 1` on False.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `deque((v, 0) for v in (v1, v2) if v)`
A queue of `(list, next_index)` pairs, one per non-empty list
Skips empty lists up front, so the queue never holds a finished list
Take the list whose turn it is
If the list has more items, put it back at the END with its index advanced
`hasNext` is true while any list still has items

p: `v1 = [1,2]`, `v2 = [3,4,5,6]`. Each `next()` pops the front pair, re-queues it if it has more, and returns the element.

blocks.h: Why a queue of pairs and not two index variables?
p: With two lists a toggle flag works, but the toggle logic grows messy once one list runs out. The queue naturally drops finished lists and generalises to k lists (the usual follow-up) without changing a line.

bullets: Time: O(1) per `next` / `hasNext`.
Space: O(k) for k lists (the queue holds one entry per unfinished list).

281.takeaway: Zigzag/round-robin iteration over k lists: keep a queue of (list, index); pop one, re-append it if it has more.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The element that the NEXT call to `next()` will return, already fetched from the underlying iterator
Replaces the underlying `hasNext()`, which has already moved past the buffered element
Pull one element ahead, or `None` at the end
Returns the buffered value, then refills the buffer
Returns the buffer without touching the iterator
This is why it is O(1) and repeatable

p: Underlying iterator over `[1,2,3]`. The columns show the buffer after each call.

blocks.h: Why prefetch instead of calling `iterator.next()` inside `peek`?
p: A basic iterator can't undo `next()`. If `peek` consumed an element, a later `next()` would skip it. Keeping the element in `self.nxt` means it is consumed from the underlying iterator exactly once, but can be read many times.

bullets: Time: O(1) per call.
Space: O(1), one buffered element.

284.takeaway: Peeking iterator: always keep one element prefetched; `peek` reads the buffer, `next` returns it and refills.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Treat each index as a node with an edge to `nums[index]`; values are in 1..n so every edge stays inside the array
Turning an array into a linked list with a cycle
The two meet somewhere inside the cycle
`slow = nums[0]`, then both one step at a time
The meeting point of the second phase is the cycle's entrance, which is the duplicate

p: `nums = [1,3,4,2,2]`: the pointer path is 1 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 2 → 4… The duplicate 2 is where two different indices (3 and 4) lead into the same node.

blocks.h: Why is the cycle entrance the duplicate?
p: The array has n+1 entries with values in 1..n, so by pigeonhole two indices share a value; that node has two incoming edges, which can only happen at the entrance of the cycle (other cycle nodes have one incoming edge from the cycle and none from outside). Floyd's phase 2 returns to this node: the distance from the start to the entrance equals the distance from the meeting point to the entrance (mod cycle length).
Starting both pointers at `nums[0]` instead of index 0 is equivalent: index 0 is never in the cycle (no value equals 0), so it acts as the 'tail' that leads into the cycle.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(1), the input is read-only.

287.takeaway: Find the duplicate by treating the array as a linked list with a cycle; Floyd's tortoise and hare finds the cycle entrance in O(n) time and O(1) space.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Splits on any whitespace into a list of words
Early exit; also guards `zip`, which would silently truncate
The other direction: two letters must not map to the same word
Returns the existing value for `k`, or stores `v` and returns it
Insert-if-absent and read in one call
If the stored mapping disagrees with the current pair, the pattern fails

p: `pattern = "abba"`, `s = "dog cat cat dog"`.
A one-way map accepts `pattern = "ab"`, `s = "dog dog"`: a→dog, b→dog, both consistent. But different letters must map to different words (a bijection), which only the reverse map `m2` can check.
Compare first-occurrence index patterns: `[pattern.index(p) for p in pattern] == [w.index(x) for x in w]`. Same idea, but `index` is O(n) each, giving O(n²).

bullets: Time: O(n) for n words.
Space: O(n) for the two maps.

290.takeaway: Word pattern is a bijection check: keep letter→word and word→letter maps and make sure both stay consistent.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Row and column of every 1 (house), collected separately
Manhattan distance splits into independent row and column parts
Collected in row-major order, so the row indexes are non-decreasing
No sort needed for rows, but `cols` must be sorted
The median minimises the sum of absolute differences
Total Manhattan distance to the meeting point

p: Houses at rows [0, 0, 2] and columns [0, 4, 2]. Sorted columns: [0, 2, 4]. The medians are row 0 and column 2.

For points on a line, moving the meeting point one step past the median brings it closer to fewer points than it moves away from, so the total distance grows. The median balances the two sides. Manhattan distance is |dx| + |dy|, so rows and columns can be optimised independently.
The mean minimises squared distance, not absolute distance. A far outlier drags the mean but not the median: columns `[0, 0, 100]` have median 0 (total 100) but mean 33 (total 133 + ...).

bullets: Time: O(m·n + h log h) where h is the number of houses (the sort of columns).
Space: O(h).
blocks.p: The mean minimises squared distance, not absolute distance. For columns `[0, 0, 100]` the median 0 gives total 100, but meeting at the mean (33) gives 33 + 33 + 67 = 133.

296.takeaway: Best meeting point under Manhattan distance: the median of the row coordinates and the median of the column coordinates, independently.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Union-Find (disjoint set) forest: each land cell points to a representative; a root points to itself
Connectivity that changes by adding items
Follow parents to the root, halving the path as you go (path compression)
Cell is already land: a repeated addition changes nothing
Assume the new cell is its own island
Union with each land neighbour; every successful merge reduces the island count by one
A sparse map avoids allocating an m×n array of parents
Few land cells in a huge grid

blocks.h: Why Union-Find and not DFS after every addition?
p: Re-running a flood-fill after each of k additions costs O(k·m·n). Union-Find handles each addition in nearly O(1): it only checks the four neighbours.
Union-Find only supports merging, which matches this problem exactly: land is only added, never removed. The "Number of Islands II" structure would not work if cells could turn back into water.

bullets: Time: O(k · α) per addition ≈ O(k) total, for k positions.
Space: O(k) for the parent dict.

305.takeaway: Online connectivity with additions: Union-Find; each new land cell counts +1 and each successful union with a neighbour counts -1.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Dimensions: A is m×kk, B is kk×n
For each non-zero `A[i][k]`, add its contribution to a whole row of the result
Reordering the classic i-j-k loops so zeros can be skipped early
Skips the entire inner loop for a zero entry
Sparse inputs: this saves most of the work
Skips zero entries of B too

p: `A = [[1,0,0],[-1,0,3]]`, `B = [[7,0,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,1]]`. Only products where both entries are non-zero are computed.

blocks.h: Why does the loop order matter?
p: The textbook order `i, j, k` computes each result cell with a dot product and multiplies every pair, zero or not: m·kk·n multiplications. With `i, k, j` the zero check on `A[i][k]` lets you skip a whole length-n inner loop at once. The result is the same, only the work changes.

bullets: Time: O(nnz(A) · n) in the worst case, instead of O(m·kk·n).
Space: O(m·n) for the result.

311.takeaway: Sparse matrix multiply: loop i, k, j and skip zero entries so only non-zero products are computed.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Column index → list of values; missing columns start as empty lists
Grouping by a key without `if key not in`
BFS queue of (node, column) pairs; root is column 0
Carrying extra state with each node
Column offset relative to the root
Visits level by level, so within a column the values come top to bottom
Required vertical order within a column

p: Tree `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`. BFS order is 3, 9, 20, 15, 7; the dict after each visit:

A DFS may reach a deeper node in a column before a shallower one that sits in the same column on another branch, giving the wrong top-to-bottom order. BFS processes shallower nodes first, so each column list is ordered by depth (and left to right within the same depth).

head: Approach
Column order top→bottom correct?
Extra
rows: needs row tracking and sorting by (col, row)

blocks.h: Why sort the keys rather than track min/max column?
p: Sorting k column keys costs O(k log k), while tracking `min_col`/`max_col` and iterating the range avoids the sort and gives O(n). Both are acceptable; mention the O(n) variant as the follow-up.

bullets: Time: O(n + k log k) where k is the number of columns (O(n) overall with min/max tracking).
Space: O(n).

314.takeaway: Vertical order = BFS with (node, column) pairs and a dict from column to values; sort the column keys at the end.
